slides.1.title: 🌞 Overview of Italy’s “Wine Cellar”
slides.1.content:
Apulia (Italian: Puglia) forms the heel of the Italian “boot” and is Italy’s easternmost region, bordered by the Adriatic Sea to the east and the Ionian Sea to the south; the Gargano peninsula is the “spur” and the Salento peninsula the “heel”. Puglia is one of Italy’s largest wine producers, and one of its largest producers of bulk and rosé wine.

🌞 One of Italy’s warmest and driest regions, with a full Mediterranean climate; the land is flat, with only about 2% mountains — the least mountainous region of Italy.

slides.3.title: 🍇 Primitivo — Puglia’s Star
slides.3.content:
🧬 Known in Puglia since the 17th century. In the 1990s Primitivo was shown to be genetically identical to America’s Zinfandel, and in 2000 both were shown to be identical to Croatia’s Crljenak Kaštelanski (Tribidrag). The name is often said to come from “primo” (first), referring to its early ripening. Traditionally trained as alberello and used as vino da taglio (bulk blending wine); deep colour, high alcohol, full body and concentrated fruit.

🏔️ Elegant style

Benchmark: Gioia del Colle DOC (Murge plateau, 200-450 m)

Flavours: red berries, spice, herbs, minerality

Soils: shallow, calcareous, iron-rich reddish clay over limestone

Style: high acidity; less powerful, more refined and elegant than Manduria

Riserva aged 2 years

🍷 Rich, jammy style

Benchmark: Primitivo di Manduria DOC / Dolce Naturale DOCG

Flavours: blackberry jam, prunes, chocolate, liquorice

Terrain: Salento faces the Ionian Sea; mostly flat, with reddish iron-rich sandy clay over limestone

Style: rich, powerful, full-bodied

The best-known internationally
slides.4.title: 🏆 Primitivo’s Two Main Areas
slides.4.content:
Primitivo’s two main areas are Manduria and Gioia del Colle: Manduria is flat, near the sea, powerful and rich; Gioia del Colle sits on the Murge plateau at higher elevation, with higher acidity and more refinement.

🍷 Primitivo di Manduria DOC (1975)

  • Location: Salento, southern Puglia, facing the Ionian Sea; mostly flat
  • Soils: reddish, iron-rich sandy clay over limestone
  • Rules: alberello-trained vines; min. 85% Primitivo (most is 100%)
  • Riserva: min. 2 years’ ageing (9 months in wood)

🍯 Primitivo di Manduria Dolce Naturale DOCG (2011)

  • Status: Puglia’s first DOCG
  • Grape: 100% Primitivo
  • Winemaking: grapes harvested overripe on the vine or lightly air-dried after harvest
  • Residual sugar: min. 5% (50 g/L)
  • Area: the same as Primitivo di Manduria DOC

🏔️ Gioia del Colle DOC

  • Location: the Murge plateau, gentle hills at 200-450 m
  • Soils: shallow, calcareous, iron-rich reddish clay over limestone
  • Main wine: varietal Primitivo; Riserva min. 2 years
  • Style: high acidity; less powerful, more refined and elegant than Manduria
slides.5.title: 🖤 Negroamaro — the Soul of Salento
slides.5.content:
🖤 Negroamaro: the soul of Salento

Negroamaro (Negro Amaro) is a traditional (possibly native) grape of Puglia, grown mainly in Salento. Its name is usually explained as “black” + “bitter” (amaro), though some say it means “double black”. There is also an early-ripening biotype, Negro Amaro Precoce.

🍇 High sugar, good acidity

High sugar levels (high alcohol) with good acidity; reliable, adaptable and drought-resistant.

IWS: Reliable, adaptable, drought-resistant
🌸 Extremely versatile

Light, fruity reds; intense rosati; full-bodied, structured, robust reds — it can do them all, and it is the main grape of Salento rosato.

Leone de Castris’s Five Roses (Cinque Rose)
🍷 Main appellations

Salice Salentino DOC is the main appellation for Negroamaro (min. 75%, often with a little Malvasia Nera di Brindisi/Lecce); Copertino DOC is also Negroamaro-based, giving sturdy reds.

Salice Salentino and Copertino
slides.6.title: ⚪ Puglia’s White Wines
slides.6.content:
🍾 Bombino Bianco (San Severo DOC)

Thought to be native to Puglia and widespread in the north and centre; naturally high in acidity, it is ideal for sparkling wine.

  • Note: not a mutation of Bombino Nero — no genetic relation has been proven
  • Appellation: San Severo DOC (Puglia’s first DOC) is known for Bombino Bianco sparkling wine
  • Also: one of the white grapes blended into Cacc'e mmitte di Lucera

🌿 Verdeca (Locorotondo, Martina Franca DOC)

A native Apulian white grape whose name relates to “verde” (green); the star of the whites of the Valle d'Itria (the valley of the trulli).

  • Appellations: Locorotondo DOC, Martina Franca DOC
  • Partner: Bianco d'Alessano
  • Style: fresh, lemon, green apple, almond

🌼 Minutolo (Fiano Aromatico) and others

Minutolo, also called Fiano Aromatico, is an aromatic white grape of the Valle d'Itria, distinct from Campania’s Fiano.

  • Moscato di Trani DOC: sweet wines from Moscato Bianco (locally called Moscato Reale)
  • Castel del Monte Bianco: Pampanuto, Bombino Bianco and others
  • International varieties: less than 5%
slides.7.title: 🏰 Castel del Monte — Four Appellations
slides.7.content:
🍷 Castel del Monte Nero di Troia Riserva DOCG

Min. 90% Nero di Troia and min. 2 years’ ageing (1 year in wood). Castel del Monte lies on the Murge plateau in central Puglia, with shallow, stony topsoils of clay over limestone bedrock — the home of Nero di Troia.

Thick skin, high tannin, moderate acidity; less powerful than Primitivo and Negroamaro

Producers: Rivera (Il Falcone, Castel del Monte Rosso Riserva) · Torrevento (Vigna Pedale)

🏆 Castel del Monte Rosso Riserva DOCG

Min. 65% Nero di Troia, blended with Aglianico and Montepulciano; min. 2 years’ ageing (1 year in wood). Note: it is not 100% Nero di Troia.

Nero di Troia was traditionally blended because of its tannins

Related grapes: Aglianico and Montepulciano also grow here

🌸 Castel del Monte Bombino Nero DOCG

A DOCG dedicated to rosato: min. 90% Bombino Nero. Bombino Nero is thin-skinned, high in acidity and low in sugar, and considered native around Castel del Monte (Andria).

Lighter and less structured than Negroamaro rosati

Key fact: Puglia’s only appellation strictly for rosato

⚪ Castel del Monte DOC

The widest range of wines and styles: reds from Nero di Troia, Aglianico and Montepulciano; rosati from Bombino Nero, Nero di Troia and Aglianico; and whites. The nearby octagonal Castel del Monte, built by Frederick II in the 13th century, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Red, rosé and white

Producer: Tormaresca (Bocca di Lupo is an Aglianico)
slides.8.title: 🍽️ Puglia Food and Wine Pairing
slides.8.content:
Puglia’s cuisine is built on olive oil, tomatoes, handmade orecchiette, seafood and wild greens — simple in style, with excellent ingredients. Burrata and orecchiette are Puglia’s great gifts to the world’s table.

🍝 Orecchiette con Cime di Rapa × Primitivo / Negroamaro

Ear-shaped pasta with bitter turnip tops is Puglia’s most iconic dish. Fruity Primitivo or herbal Negroamaro both balance the bitterness; old-vine Primitivo from Manduria is the best match.

🐙 Polpo alla Pignata × Negroamaro Rosato

Octopus stewed in a clay pot (a Salento tradition) with Negroamaro rosato, whose herbal notes echo the seafood’s minerality. Leone de Castris’s Five Roses is the top choice.

🧀 Burrata × Verdeca (Locorotondo DOC)

Puglia’s creamy cheese with the local fresh Verdeca white, whose acidity cuts through the cream — a quintessential Apulian summer pairing.

🥩 Roast lamb / horse-meat salsiccia × Primitivo di Manduria

Traditional Apulian red-meat dishes with rich Primitivo di Manduria, whose tannins cut through the fat — a festive local pairing and a snapshot of rural food culture.
slides.9.title: 📜 Puglia Wine History in Depth
slides.9.content:
From an exporter of wine in Greek and Roman times, to the 20th-century capital of bulk wine, to a shift towards quality from the 1990s.

“Puglia is still one of Italy’s largest producers of bulk wine: about half of its production is wine without origin.”

Antiquity

🏺 Greeks and Romans

The Greeks brought alberello bush training; in Roman times vast amounts of wine were shipped from Apulian ports to the expanding empire, and Puglia thrived.

Middle Ages

🏰 The Crusades and Frederick II

During the Crusades of the 11th-12th centuries the wine trade and exports flourished; in the 13th century Frederick II, King of Sicily (“Puer Apuliae”, son of Puglia), built Castel del Monte.

1880s-1950s

🐛 Phylloxera and bulk wine

When phylloxera ravaged Europe in the late 19th century, Puglia planted heavily and production soared; phylloxera only reached Puglia in the 1920s. In the 1950s Puglia produced vast amounts of vino da taglio (bulk blending wine), and tendone trellises were introduced in the early 20th century.

1980s-today

🚀 Vine pull and transformation

EU vine-pull programmes in the 1980s greatly reduced old alberello vines; from the 1990s Puglia gradually shifted towards quality. Today less than 20% is bottled as DOC/G.

slides.10.title: 🧬 Primitivo vs Zinfandel: One Grape, Two Souls
slides.10.content:
🔬 DNA research: one grape, many names

Primitivo (Italy), Zinfandel (USA), and Crljenak Kaštelanski and Tribidrag (Croatia) are the same grape. Primitivo has been known in Puglia since the 17th century.

🧬 DNA milestones

Scientific identification

  • 17th century: Primitivo already known in Puglia
  • 1990s: Primitivo shown to be genetically identical to Zinfandel
  • 2000: both shown to be identical to Croatia’s Crljenak Kaštelanski (Tribidrag)
  • Exam point: Bombino Nero is not a synonym for Primitivo

Primitivo in Puglia

  • Tradition: alberello-trained and shipped north as vino da taglio for blending
  • Style: deep colour, high alcohol, full body, concentrated fruit
  • Areas: Manduria and Gioia del Colle

🍷 Three names compared

🇭🇷 Crljenak Kaštelanski / Tribidrag

The Croatian names; Croatia is considered the grape’s place of origin.

Origin
🇮🇹 Primitivo (Puglia)

Hot, dry Salento and the Murge plateau: concentrated fruit and high alcohol; Manduria is powerful, Gioia del Colle elegant.

Benchmark: Primitivo di Manduria DOC
🇺🇸 Zinfandel (California)

The same grape’s Californian name, made in styles from rich reds to White Zinfandel rosé.

Benchmarks: Sonoma, Lodi and others
slides.11.title: 🌞 Puglia Terroir in Depth
slides.11.content:
🌊 The heel of the Italian boot: Puglia is one of Italy’s warmest and driest regions, with a full Mediterranean climate; Salento is the hottest area. The landscape is mostly large undulating calcareous plateaus, broad plains and low hills, with only about 2% mountains.

🏔️

North and centre

  • Tavoliere delle Puglie: in the north, Italy’s second-largest plain, with alluvial soils on the flatter areas
  • The Murge plateau: a large calcareous karst (carsico) plateau in the centre, characterised by caves and sinkholes, with calcareous soils
  • Appellations: Castel del Monte (Nero di Troia, Bombino Nero), Gioia del Colle (Primitivo), San Severo (Bombino Bianco)
🌊

The Salento peninsula in the south

  • Climate: Puglia’s hottest area, facing both the Ionian and Adriatic seas
  • Soils: calcareous sandy clay over limestone subsoil; terra rossa (red soil rich in iron oxide)
  • Appellations: Primitivo di Manduria, Salice Salentino, Copertino — the heartland of Negroamaro

🌱 Training systems

🌿 Alberello

Widely used since ancient times (brought by the Greeks); greatly reduced after the EU vine-pull programme but still important in certain areas such as the south; Primitivo thrives with it

🍇 Tendone

Adopted in the early 20th century, particularly for bulk wine and table grapes; still used in parts of the north and centre

✂️ Cordone speronato

Modern spur-pruned cordon training

💧 Drainage

Terra rossa is well drained, with low water-holding capacity
slides.12.title: 🖤 Negroamaro and the Appellations of Salento
slides.12.content:
🖤 Negroamaro in Salento

The grape

  • Origin: a traditional (possibly native) grape of Puglia
  • Traits: high sugar (high alcohol) with good acidity; reliable, adaptable, drought-resistant
  • Main area: Salento
  • Partner: often blended with Malvasia Nera di Brindisi/Lecce

Salento’s appellations

  • Salice Salentino DOC: the main appellation for Negroamaro, on deep, calcareous sandy clay of marine origin
  • Copertino DOC: sturdy Negroamaro-based reds, also as Riserva
  • Negroamaro di Terra d'Otranto DOC: a broad appellation covering Salento
  • Salento IGT: used by many fine wines

🍷 Three styles of Negroamaro

🌸 Rosato

Negroamaro-based Salento rosato is darker than most other rosés (e.g. Chiaretto). Leone de Castris’s Five Roses was Italy’s first commercially bottled rosato.

Salice Salentino Rosato is Negroamaro-based
🍷 Salice Salentino Rosso

Min. 75% Negroamaro with a little Malvasia Nera di Brindisi/Lecce; Riserva min. 2 years (6 months in wood).

The byword for Negroamaro
🏺 Graticciaia: dried-grape concentration

Agricole Vallone makes it from air-dried (appassimento) Negroamaro, in a style akin to Amarone; a benchmark Salento IGT.

Appassimento in the south
slides.13.title: 🍾 Apulian Rosato and Winemaking Traditions
slides.13.content:
🌸 Apulian rosato: Puglia is one of Italy’s largest rosé producers, significant in both quality and quantity. Historically known as “Lagrimas”, it was first commercially bottled in the 1940s, and it is darker than most other rosés (e.g. Chiaretto).

🌸 Rosato grapes

  • North and centre: Bombino Nero
  • Salento: Negroamaro
  • Others: Primitivo, Malvasia Nera di Brindisi/Lecce
  • Bombino Nero: thin-skinned, high acid, low sugar; lighter than Negroamaro rosati
  • Salasso: “bleeding the tank” — drawing off juice from a red-wine vat to make rosato

🍷 Apulian winemaking traditions

  • Vino da taglio: bulk wine once shipped north for blending
  • Appassimento: drying grapes, e.g. Graticciaia
  • Dolce Naturale: naturally sweet wine from overripe or lightly dried Primitivo
  • Metodo classico: sparkling wine from high-acid Bombino Bianco
  • Severino Garofano: an important oenologist in Salento

slides.14.title: 🏆 Puglia’s Legendary Estates (Part 1)
slides.14.content:
🍷 From “Italy’s wine cellar” to the fine-wine stage: from the 1990s Puglia gradually shifted towards quality, and a group of estates put Primitivo and Negroamaro on the world wine map. Leone de Castris’s history and Gianfranco Fino’s ultra-premium wines represent Puglia’s two extremes.

LD

est. 1665

Leone de Castris 🏛️

Standing: a historic Salento estate and rosato pioneer

Location: Salice Salentino

Hallmark: launched “Five Roses” (Cinque Rose) in 1943, Italy’s first commercially bottled rosato

• Five Roses Rosato: €8-12 (Italy’s first commercially bottled rosato)

• Donna Lisa Salice Salentino Riserva: €15-25

• Villa Santera Primitivo di Manduria: €18-28

Tip: Five Roses is the best way into Puglia — great value and a summer essential

GF

est. 2004

Gianfranco Fino 👑

Standing: the face of fine Primitivo; Es is one of Puglia’s most sought-after wines

Location: Manduria; old alberello vines

Hallmark: a small, low-yield fine-wine estate

• Es Primitivo di Manduria: €60-100

• Jo (Negroamaro, Salento IGT): €30-50

Tip: Es is best after a few years in bottle

Tormaresca 🔬

📍 Two estates in north and south Puglia (Castel del Monte and Salento)

Owned by the Antinori family, a symbol of modernisation

Masseria Maime Negroamaro: €18-28

Bocca di Lupo Aglianico (Castel del Monte): €20-30

Ageing: 5-12 years

📍 Cellino San Marco (Brindisi province)

The Falvo family’s (Avignonesi) estate in Salento

Salento IGT range: €15-22

slides.15.title: 🍷 Puglia’s Fine Estates (Part 2) and Price Guide
slides.15.content:
🍷 Traditionalists and appassimento: Taurino holds to the tradition of long ageing in large casks, while Agricole Vallone uses appassimento to make a southern Italian take on Amarone; together they show the depth of Apulian wine culture.

TA

Guagnano

Taurino 🏺

Standing: a traditionalist benchmark in Salento, famed for long-lived Negroamaro

Location: Guagnano, Lecce province (the Salice Salentino area)

Hallmark: worked with oenologist Severino Garofano; Patriglione is made from late-harvested Negroamaro and ages for a long time

• Patriglione Salento IGT (Negroamaro): €30-50

• Salice Salentino Riserva: €10-15 (entry level)

Tip: Patriglione needs at least 10 years to show complex leather and truffle notes — a long-term cellar pick

AV

est. 1934

Agricole Vallone 🌿

Standing: a historic Salento estate; Graticciaia is the benchmark for appassimento in the south

Location: Lecce

Hallmark: Graticciaia is made from air-dried Negroamaro, in a style akin to Amarone; the winemaker was Severino Garofano

• Graticciaia Salento IGT: €30-50 (small production)

• Vigna Flaminio Brindisi Rosso: €12-18 (everyday wine)

Surprise: Graticciaia is Puglia’s most distinctive wine — appassimento gives Negroamaro a whole new dimension

A-Mano 🇺🇸

📍 Contract growers across Puglia

Founded by American winemaker Mark Shannon; a fruity, easy-drinking modern style

slides.16.title: 🍽️ Puglia Food Pairing & Baroque Wine Route
slides.16.content:
🌾 The Apulian table

Puglia’s cuisine is simple, with excellent ingredients, built on three pillars: olive oil, handmade pasta and fresh seafood. Burrata (created in Puglia in 1956) and orecchiette are Puglia’s two enduring gifts to world cuisine.

🍝 Orecchiette con Cime di Rapa × Primitivo di Manduria / Negroamaro

“Little ears with turnip tops” is Puglia’s soul food. The bitter greens are balanced by Primitivo’s jammy fruit, while Negroamaro’s herbal side brings out the freshness of the vegetables.

🐙 Polpo alla Pignata × Negroamaro Rosato / Locorotondo Bianco

Clay-pot octopus is Taranto’s traditional soul food. Negroamaro rosato’s herbal notes echo the seafood’s minerality; for something fresher, choose Locorotondo Bianco — a rare successful “rosé with seafood” match.

🧀 Burrata + tomatoes × Verdeca (Locorotondo DOC)

Puglia’s creamy cheese, created in 1956, with fresh Verdeca: the high acidity cuts the cream and the minerality echoes the tomatoes — Puglia’s perfect summer starter.

🥩 Agnello alla Brace × Primitivo di Manduria Riserva

Festive charcoal-grilled lamb with Manduria Riserva: the tannins cut the fat and the dark-fruit jam answers the char — the most moving snapshot of southern Italian country cooking.

🏛️ Puglia’s UNESCO and Baroque wine route

🏠 Alberobello (the trulli): a UNESCO World Heritage village of conical stone houses in the Valle d'Itria, surrounded by the Verdeca white-wine country of Locorotondo and Martina Franca DOC
🏰 Castel del Monte: Frederick II’s octagonal castle (UNESCO); the Rivera winery is nearby, so you can visit the castle and taste Il Falcone (Castel del Monte Rosso Riserva) on the same day
🌆 Lecce, capital of the Baroque: southern Italy’s most beautiful Baroque city, surrounded by Salice Salentino DOC; Leone de Castris welcomes visitors by appointment
🌊 Otranto and the Adriatic coast: a Byzantine-mosaic cathedral and crystal-blue bays, with fried seafood and Verdeca — the perfect end to a Salento summer

slides.19.questions.5.options.0: A. Castel del Monte Rosso Riserva DOCG
slides.19.questions.5.options.1: B. Castel del Monte Bombino Nero DOCG
slides.19.questions.5.explanation: Castel del Monte Bombino Nero DOCG is dedicated to rosato, with min. 90% Bombino Nero; Bombino Nero is thin-skinned, high in acidity and low in sugar.
slides.19.questions.6.question: Which is NOT a synonym for Primitivo?
slides.19.questions.6.explanation: Primitivo, Zinfandel, Crljenak Kaštelanski and Tribidrag are the same grape; Bombino Nero is a different variety used for rosato around Castel del Monte.
slides.19.questions.7.question: In Cacc'e mmitte di Lucera DOC, which grape is commonly blended with Nero di Troia?
slides.19.questions.7.explanation: Cacc'e mmitte di Lucera DOC is mainly Nero di Troia blended with 15-30% white grapes, including Bombino Bianco, Trebbiano Toscano and Malvasia Bianca — a red made from red and white grapes.
slides.19.questions.8.question: What is salasso?
slides.19.questions.8.options.3: D. “Bleeding the tank”, a rosé method
slides.19.questions.8.explanation: Salasso means “bleeding the tank”: drawing off part of the juice from a red-wine vat to make rosato. Puglia is one of Italy’s largest rosé producers.
slides.19.questions.9.question: Which Puglia appellation is known for Bombino Bianco-based sparkling wines?
slides.19.questions.9.options.2: C. Cacc'e mmitte di Lucera DOC
slides.19.questions.9.explanation: San Severo DOC, Puglia’s first DOC, is known for Bombino Bianco-based sparkling wines; Bombino Bianco’s naturally high acidity makes it ideal for sparkling wine.
